Posted November 25, 2002

Analysis by Richard Cowan
Let me begin by saying that I am a libertarian and as such I oppose almost all censorship, with only such special exceptions as child pornography and direct incitement to violence. So this is not about censorship. I am not advocating the enactment of any law that would give any government more control over the media. I trust governments even less.

Nonetheless, as regular readers know all to well, I like to say that the best two-word explanation for cannabis prohibition is bad journalism. I have gone to great lengths to prove this point.
See
 Classic Reefer Madness At London Times: " Woman who killed father 'driven mad by cannabis.' " Quacks and Hacks and Schizophrenia. Is It Paranoid to Distrust Politicized Science?
and
 Mormon Church Newspaper Violates The Ninth Commandment. Gives False Evidence Against Marijuana Users and Anti-Prohibitionists.
and
 Does Reporting on Marijuana Lower The Media's IQ (Integrity Quotient)?
and
 Marijuana Prohibition, Media Criticism, Copyrights and the 8th and 9th Commandments

Last week the Internet, in its wonderful way, brought up several stories that made it clear that I need to be more specific. I think that I have made very clear what I mean by bad journalism, but bad is very general in its meaning.

While John Walters was speaking to the Vancouver Board of Trade people sitting at Marc Emery's table shouted Liar when he was lying, which was most of the time.
See
 Dan Forbes Documents Walters Lies About Potency. Understanding That The War On Cannabis Is Built On Lies Is Key to Understanding More Than Just Drug War.
and links

However, it was Walters response that made me conclude that bad was not sufficiently explicit description of journalistic handling of the cannabis issues. He said, " I'm a public official. I am subject to the scrutiny of the press and the Congress . . . I've never heard of you. "

The scrutiny of the press Pause for laughter. Pause for a powerful anti-emetic!

Who knew that he was such a comedian?

In fact, a few editorial pages, notably in the Vancouver Sun and the Las Vegas Review Journal, have challenged some of his more obviously dishonest claims. But for the most part they simply report whatever he says without providing either context or even readily available facts.
See
 If the Las Vegas Review Journal " Gets It, " Why Don't The Other Papers?

But to top it all off, Robert Matas in The Globe and Mail, one of Canada's two national newspapers reported that in an interview in Vancouver Walters said, Marijuana poses a greater danger to the United States than heroin, cocaine or amphetamines.

That is not the first time that he has said something like this, but here it is more explicit.
See
 Marijuana Bigger Problem Than Meth? DEAland And The Bush Administration Have a Very Serious Walters Problem. We Couldn't Make This Up!

How many newspaper editors believe that? But will any actually question this bizarre strategic premise for the Drug War. "?

That made me think about journalistic negligencebecause negligence is a well-defined legal term that has redefined the relationship between clients/patients/customers and those who are charging them for a product or service.

Buyer beware has increasingly become seller beware. However, as the application of tort law (civil damage cases) has spread to more and more areas, the media have been left virtually exempt, except in the obvious case of libel.

West's Encyclopedia of American Lawsays, A person has acted negligently if he or she has departed from the conduct expected of a reasonably prudent person acting under similar circumstances.To establish negligence, a plaintiff must prove that the defendant had a duty to the plaintiff, the defendant breached that duty by failing to conform to the required standard of conduct, the defendant's negligent conduct was the cause of the harm to the plaintiff, and the plaintiff was, in fact, harmed or damaged Gradually the law began to imply a promise to exercise care or skill in the performance of certain services.

There are two points here.

First, it is quite clear that much of the media do not exercise the proper care in performing their duties in a way that a reasonable person would expect, while they charge readers for bringing them reliable news.

They do not even meet their own self-proclaimed (self-promoting) standards by which they sell their services. At least when the subject is cannabis, they overlook such basic concepts as fact checking about points which are easily verified.
See
 Canada's National Post Prints DEAland Prohibitionist Propaganda and Ignores Facts. Even Anti-Prohibitionists Have No Standards When the Subject Is Cannabis. Analysis by Richard Cowan

This carelessness, negligence, harms the public in general and specific groups in particular.

In this context, I can imagine patients suing a newspaper or other media outlets for negligence and damages for interfering in their obtaining access to medical cannabis.
See
 The Denver Post Editorial Page Lies to Its Readers About Medical Marijuana Again

Non-medical users or the families of prisoners might sue if they can establish a connection between negligent journalism and harsher penalties. Alas, there are almost endless examples here, if not legal opportunities.

Second, even if it is not possible to bring legal action against the media for negligence in particular instances, it is an important moral concept, especially in an industry that so often demands that others be held accountable for their negligence.

Moreover, while bad journalism and negligent journalism often overlap they are not entirely the same thing. For example, a very brief item that reports that the British Lung Foundation published a report claiming that cannabis harms the lungs may be bad in that it tells the readers too little, but it would not necessarily be negligent because papers cannot be expected to report on every subject exhaustively. On the other hand, a more complete report might be negligent because it expands on the claims in the BLF report uncritically.
See
 British Lung Foundation Cons Media. Blaming Cannabis for Problems Caused By Prohibition. Tripping Over the Party Line. The Media Fell For It, As Usual, But UK Anti-Tobacco Group Does Not.

Also it would not be reasonable to hold every publication to the same standards. Not every newspaper is the New York Times, thank God.
See
 How Prohibitionism Corrupts the New York Times: Educating the Children with the Party Line, and Undermining Journalistic Integrity. Analysis by Richard Cowan.
and numerous links.

Speaking of the New York Times, last week the Associated Press carried a story by Michelle R. Smith that had no mention of cannabis, but was quite unintentionally hilarious.

It seems that Howell Raines, the Times' executive editor, told a panel on journalism that If the Bush administration puts out false information, the Times will report it, but the paper has an obligation to follow through with more stories analyzing the information. Of course, he was talking about the Middle East, not cannabis.

The article went on to report, Raines elicited groans from some in the audience when he said the Times was not wrong when it reported on Oct. 27 that thousands of protesters attended a peace march in Washington the previous day, fewer than organizers hoped for. The first story was incomplete, Raines said. The number was a judgment matter ... a matter of scope.

But, he added, " In this business there's only one thing to do when you're wrong and that's 'get it right' as soon as you can. "

Yeah, sure. This is a newspaper that has never reported the huge increase in cannabis possession arrests under Rudy Giuliani.
See
 Giuliani's Police State Like the Marijuana Prohibition That He Loves Is A Counterproductive Fraud. 3 Articles.

But they are worried about how many people were in a parade in Washington. Such numbers are notoriously difficult to estimate, but arrest data are available from their own police.
See
 Marches Reported Around the World, Arrests In New York, Peace In The UK, Fear In San Francisco, but An Odd Silence in Vancouver.

Raines praised a recent front page story about Britney Spears, saying, " It was about the fame machine, the economic engine that's behind it Our readers are interested in reading a sophisticated exegesis of a sociological phenomenon like that.

But they are not interested in how many New Yorkers are arrested over a period of eight years?

Nor are they interested in the fact that the Drug Czar is claiming, Marijuana poses a greater danger to the United States than heroin, cocaine or amphetamines.???

There will be no sophisticated exegesis of a sociological phenomenon about that.

Which brings us back to the legal definition of negligence: failing to conform to the required standard of conduct.

If the law began to imply a promise to exercise care or skill in the performance of certain services, then does none of this apply to the industry that has more impact on the quality of life, public and private, than any other?

And if it does not apply to the New York Times, to whom would it apply? It is not that they are the worst, by no means. In fact, they are far better than the Washington Post.
See
 The Washington Post and The Evil of Banality. " Only the hypocrite is really rotten to the core.

However, the motto of the New York Times is All the News That Is Fit To Print and the executive editor boasts about sophisticated exegesis of a sociological phenomenon about Britney Spears!

Can it be that, given these claims, this self-promoting puffery, they have no legal obligations to either their readers who buy their papers or the victims of their negligence, the hundreds of thousands who were arrested under Giuliani without the Times saying a word?

Indeed, it is all too easy to prove that the Times contributed to the atmosphere of hatred toward cannabis users that made this possible. And yet they have legal impunity? Perhaps, but they do not have moral impunity.

Frankly, I hope that some enterprising tort lawyers will find a way to sue the various media outlets, even if it just gets their attention. It would be a novel but not frivolous suit.

In the meantime, it is quite obvious that we cannot trust them to perform without negligence, so we have to replace them, to go around them.

The term is disintermediation. In the broadest sense it means eliminate the middle-man and that has been one of the most successful applications of the Internet. (For a view of " authentic journalism " see Narconews.com.)

It may be impossible to sue the media, and difficult to replace them, but their negligence has given us no choice. If we fail to act, we are guilty of contributory negligence, which is to say, we will have only ourselves to blame if we rely on others to free us.
